title: Global Brands Shift About $254 Million in Orders From Bangladesh to India Amid Unrest
excerpt: Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer and Celio diverted nearly a tenth of Bangladesh's monthly orders in the first half of November as labour unrest, factory shutdowns and a wage hike eroded its cost edge, Reuters reports.
body:
• Global fashion brands including Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer and Celio diverted about $254 million in orders from Bangladesh between November 1 and 18, with most of the business moving to India, according to Reuters.
  • Labour unrest and factory shutdowns have cost Bangladesh more than $400 million in production losses, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) says, in an industry that earns over 80% of the country's export income.
  • Bangladesh approved a 36% garment minimum-wage increase on Wednesday — the smallest rise in four decades — which industry leaders say further narrows its cost edge over India.
  • For India's textile exporters, the shift is already showing up in markets: Gokaldas Exports jumped as much as 11% and Trident about 5% after the Reuters report, as buyers weigh making temporary diversions permanent.

Global fashion retailers including Zara and H&M shifted nearly a tenth of their monthly orders from Bangladesh to other Asian manufacturing hubs in the first half of November, as labour unrest disrupted production and rising costs eroded the country's competitive edge, three factory owners told Reuters. Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India — a shift the owners said could extend beyond the current unrest.

Why buyers are moving

The protests have caused more than $400 million in production losses, according to the BGMEA, in an industry that accounts for more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings and nearly 40% of its manufacturing jobs. Manufacturers around Dhaka have lost an estimated 20 to 25 production days to the disruptions, and some are considering overtime and costly air freight to meet delivery commitments.

Industry leaders said rising wages, energy shortages and political uncertainty have weakened the low-cost advantage that made Bangladesh the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China. Persistent energy shortages, exacerbated by the Middle East crisis, have forced some factories onto more expensive alternative power sources. Political tensions surrounding former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's possible return to Dhaka from India have added to concerns about further disruption.

On Wednesday, Bangladesh approved a 36% increase in the minimum wage for garment workers — the smallest rise in four decades. The increase fell well short of workers' demands to more than double wages, triggering fresh clashes with police, even as Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, called the increase "satisfactory" and said he hoped all garment workers would resume work from Saturday.

India's opening

India has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of the diversions, while buyers are also looking to Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to reduce supply-chain risks and improve delivery reliability, industry leaders said. Delivery speed is a growing part of the pitch: M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury, a director of the BGMEA, said India can offer buyers a delivery advantage of about a week, Vietnam and Cambodia can cut lead times by as much as 15 days, and rival hubs typically complete production and delivery within 60 to 90 days, compared with about 120 days in Bangladesh.

"The challenge is restoring buyers' confidence before temporary shifts become long-term sourcing decisions. Brands have options. They will not wait for us if instability persists."

— M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury, Director, BGMEA

The factory owners, speaking on condition of anonymity because of their relationships with international buyers, said the unrest prompted Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer, Celio and other brands to divert orders, with India receiving the bulk of the business. Zara owner Inditex declined to comment on Reuters' questions, while M&S, H&M and Celio did not respond to requests for comment.

Khan Monirul Alam, managing director of Alps Apparels Group, which mainly supplies European brands, said the unrest was already hitting new business: "Since November 1, most of my buyers have stopped placing orders because of the unrest. They are telling us our orders have been shifted, postponed or cancelled and that they have already found alternative solutions." BGMEA president Mahmud Hasan Khan declined to name the brands but said temporarily shifting some orders elsewhere helps the industry retain global clients while minimising financial losses.

What to watch

Indian textile shares rallied after the Reuters report, with Gokaldas Exports jumping as much as 11% and Trident gaining about 5%; Welspun Living, KPR Mill and Vardhman Textiles rose around 2% each. The open question for both countries is whether diverted orders return once Bangladesh stabilises. Factory owners warned that orders already moved could be followed by the loss of future business as buyers reassess where to source garments — and Chowdhury said buyers are increasingly prioritising delivery times over price when choosing suppliers.
nri_angle: The diversion puts more orders into India's garment hubs and lifted Indian textile stocks, a shift diaspora investors and families with ties to the apparel trade are watching.
author: Diaspora Desk
